reasoning: Every object is stored and fetched by a unique object key and the store cannot query inside the object's contents.
use_case: Storing user-uploaded photos/videos and data-lake files for an app
why: Cheap, virtually unlimited, highly durable storage where files are always fetched whole by key.
limitation: No querying inside objects; high latency vs. a database

reasoning: It stores JSON documents and can build secondary indexes and run SQL-like (N1QL/SQL++) queries on fields inside them.
use_case: User profiles and shopping carts for an e-commerce site
why: Each profile/cart is one flexible JSON document that is queried by fields and served fast from its built-in memory cache.
best_for: Flexible JSON data with fast reads
limitation: Weak at multi-document joins and complex relationships

reasoning: Data is organised by row key into column families and is built for very wide, sparse rows with millions of columns on HDFS.
use_case: Storing billions of IoT sensor readings / message history
why: Handles huge write volumes and fast range scans over a row key across a Hadoop cluster.
limitation: No secondary indexes or joins; needs Hadoop/ZooKeeper to run

reasoning: It is purpose-built to store nodes and edges and query them with graph languages like Gremlin, openCypher and SPARQL.
why: Multi-hop relationship traversals are fast, which would need many costly joins in other families.
limitation: Poor for bulk aggregation/analytics; AWS-only managed service

reasoning: It keeps arbitrary byte values in RAM indexed only by string keys, with no query language at all.
use_case: Caching database query results and web sessions
why: Sub-millisecond get/set from memory reduces load on the main database.
limitation: No persistence or replication; data lost on restart
